extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and early-career newspaper reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance from a city editor on how reporters should behave, build careers, and assess news value in a newspaper newsroom. Covers beats, specialization, relationships, promotions, planning, and the elastic nature of news judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know important people and backgrounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter should learn 'all the important people who are not on news runs but who must be handled deftly' and be able to call them by their first names; this makes him more valuable than a first-year cub who hasn't seen that particular news source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Takes more than a year to acquire these contacts. Learn who are the paper's friends and enemies; when unsure of someone's background, refer the instance to the city editor. Failing to know background can cause a reporter to be abrupt with a friend or to grant favors to an arch enemy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand local community traditions and sensitivities
rubrics_metrics.description: Every community 'has its own traditions, its own customs, its own viewpoint' so that a story acceptable in one city might 'stir up the wrath of an entire community elsewhere.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study local culture (history, literature, customs, dominant ethnic sentiments). Avoid making fun of or casting reflection on locally cherished things. A reporter cannot learn all this in a year—be cautious and consult editors when in doubt. Example: Sheboygan's German heritage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the paper's policy and personalities
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter 'can't learn all about his paper's policy until hundreds of questions have come up' in experience; regular subscribers notice departures from policy and may complain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of what the paper stands for and the publisher's and editor's likes/dislikes. Know which stories the publisher will support enthusiastically. Learn personalities (e.g., where to reach a source after hours) to cover time-sensitive assignments effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refer uncertain background or delicate cases to the city editor
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reporter 'doesn't know the background' of a subject or the paper's relationship with them, 'his only safe action is to refer to the city editor all instances' of uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the city editor's institutional memory to avoid damaging errors (e.g., giving big favors to enemies). This protects both the reporter and the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan to remain at first paper for at least three years
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice: 'plan to remain with his first paper for at least three years' because reporters learn, gain trust, and are usually treated fairly in the long run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three years lets a reporter know whether he's developing into a 'crack reporter' and gives time to earn raises comparable to metropolitan pay when cost of living is considered. Only leave early for good reason (e.g., unhappy environment or clear better opportunities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge promotion readiness by assignments and reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: By the third year a reporter will know 'whether or not he is developing into a crack reporter'—signs include getting important assignments and being relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relied upon and getting major tasks, talk with the city editor about pay/permanency. If the paper can't pay more, the editor will either ask the reporter to hang on or advise seeking greener fields; good men are usually supported rather than blocked.

rubrics_metrics.name: City editor should advance promising reporters—but cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: When a city editor 'finds a man who looks good he should try to advance that man a little more rapidly than normally is customary,' though rapid advancement has problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid raises may be resisted by business office or may cause the reporter to become overconfident and leave. Prefer candidates who like the town and are substantial rather than restless; promotion strategy balances reward and retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider cost of living and long-term opportunity before moving to bigger papers
rubrics_metrics.description: 'More money' in a metropolitan paper doesn't inevitably mean more buying power; moving to a higher salary can be a pay cut if cost of living is higher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate comparative living costs and whether the move truly advances career opportunities rather than just nominal pay. Many small offices offer demanding, challenging, and rewarding positions equivalent to big-city jobs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build deep contacts across all social strata ('news gold mines')
rubrics_metrics.description: 'These persons will be in every stratum: lawyers, Chinese laundrymen, clubwomen, truck drivers, preachers, policemen, and school teachers.' Contacts are better called 'news gold mines.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meet as many people as possible and cultivate them so they're eager to give information. Contacts provide material for consistent specialty reporting and beat coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow assignments enthusiastically and produce a usable story
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter 'has no excuse for coming back from an assignment with nothing to write, for each assignment offers three possibilities'—the expected story, an unexpected extra, or a substitute when the original plan fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always look for secondary angles and interviews; if the primary story evaporates, find why it failed and turn that into a story. Avoid returning empty-handed; think in terms of the three possible outcomes described in the chapter (1. the story the editor suggested; 2. the suggested story plus additional material; 3. a substitute story explaining why the original failed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a specialty by persistent beat reporting, but don't neglect core duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialists 'know more than anyone else in the city about a particular news field'; a cub can become a specialist (e.g., camera/photo specialist) by hunting for underserved beats and writing about them until established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build specialty material through reporting (club meetings, interviews, product news). Be persistent—submit columns and demonstrate readership interest; the editor will test stamina and audience. However, develop specialties on your own time and not by shortchanging assigned beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not trespass on other reporters' beats; respect specialty boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: 'No TRESPASSING ON MY JOB'—ace reporters are specialists and guard their fields; a newcomer must find his own regular sources and not steal assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify underserved beats rather than encroach on others. Gain acceptance by producing reliable material that fills a gap; the editor will then use your pieces. Respect colleagues' specialties to maintain newsroom harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a specialty outside regular hours—expect to work beyond forty hours
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The ambitious man usually has to do more than the boss asks before he wins recognition' and 'Roger's chances for hurry-up promotion demand forgetting about the forty-hour workweek.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacture your own luck by doing extra reporting in off-hours (attending clubs, developing contacts). But do so without neglecting regular assignments; balance extra effort with daily duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be persistent and demonstrate reader interest to win regular features
rubrics_metrics.description: Rog keeps submitting camera columns; the city editor clips readers' reactions and asks about a standing head, eventually making Rog 'the camera expert.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proposing a new feature, persist and build proof of audience interest. Editors may withhold formal commitments until satisfied a feature will be sustainable; patience and demonstrable readership can convert trial pieces into regular space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid chasing scoops that endanger assigned work
rubrics_metrics.description: The movie notion that 'the road to fame is paved with exclusive stories' is misleading; scoops of stature are usually 'broken' by experienced reporters and 'scooping the world can be highly dangerous' for a cub who abandons assignments for gossip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When on an assignment, stay with it; if you hear something else worth following, report back to the editor—if it's worth it, the editor will reassign. Wild goose chases often 'fizzle' or produce nothing and leave you to be reprimanded for missing assigned work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept editing and cuts without personal affront
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter should never regard cuts or rewriting as a personal affront; a story is 'merely a piece of copy that ran into misfortune' not a 'casus belli.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid publicly confronting copy editors; persistent grumbling brands a cub as a 'growler' and results in more scrutiny. Learn to be impersonal and wry about space judgments; consider 'slash paragraphs' strategy to protect essential material from the butcher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the future book to anticipate predictable news and manage newsroom workload
rubrics_metrics.description: The city editor keeps 'the future book,' an enormous ledger where he records the news calendar—club meetings, anniversaries, expected developments—so 'predictable' news is outlined definitely and thoroughly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult and contribute to the future book. Use out-of-town papers, calendars, and reporters' tips to populate it. When tomorrow looks heavy, defer 'can hold' items to less busy days to balance staff workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that news values are elastic and depend on competition
rubrics_metrics.description: 'News values change faster than the weather' and what a story is worth can alter quickly with competing news; there is no absolute formula for news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to 'write it tight' at one hour and 'let it run at length' later as pages change. Understand that breaking events (e.g., disasters) can suddenly re-rank all items; reporters and editors must show ingenuity and elasticity on big days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt Bleyer's working definition of news but apply timeliness flexibly
rubrics_metrics.description: 'News is anything timely that interests a number of readers, and the best news is that which has the greatest interest for the greatest number.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'timely' sensibly—stories of historical events can be newsworthy if recent revelations or context make them relevant (examples: Pershing memoirs, discovery of an explorer's camp). Avoid the extreme zeal that ranks events by minute-of-day; balance freshness with demonstrable reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use major unexpected news as the true test of staff quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The staff's ingenuity, elasticity, and durability are shown when 'an unexpected story, or several unexpected, must be cared for in stride' while not ignoring predictable news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare teams and plans for days when unpredictable events overwhelm the calendar. Maintain flexibility in assignments and page allocation; such days reveal which reporters and editors can handle pressure and reprioritization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh union vs professional organization membership carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial workers' unions (A.F. of L., C.I.O.) and professional groups (American Press Society) offer different benefits. Some cities require union membership for jobs; A.P.S. demands four years' experience for full membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If union membership is required, join. Where optional, be patient until organizational alignments settle (historical A.F. of L.-C.I.O. conflict). Consider A.P.S. for professional standards and potential career advantage; recognize apprenticeship/master distinctions in organizations.
